{
  "screen_decision": "include",
  "screen_rationale": "The text discusses the failure rate of preclinical animal studies in predicting human treatment outcomes, specifically mentioning that \"more than 80% of potential therapeutics fail when tested in people\" and that \"animal models of disease are frequently condemned as poor predictors of whether an experimental drug can become an effective treatment.\" It quantifies the concordance problem by stating that \"Eight of these compounds ultimately failed in clinical trials, which together involved thousands of people.\" This directly addresses the quantitative measure of agreement between animal results and human clinical outcomes.",
  "arm": "efficacy",
  "arm_evidence": "\"Even after animal studies suggest that a treatment will be safe and effective, more than 80% of potential therapeutics fail when tested in people.\"",
  "therapeutic_areas": [
    "neurodegeneration"
  ],
  "areas_evidence": "\"One such group of patients is those with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), the fatal neurodegenerative condition also known as Lou Gehrig’s or motor neuron disease.\"",
  "model_type": "genetic",
  "model_evidence": "\"Mouse models expressing a mutant form of the RNA binding protein TDP43 show hallmark features of ALS...\" and \"Almost 90% of the mice had an average lifespan of 134 days, give or take 10 days.\"",
  "species": [
    "mouse"
  ],
  "species_evidence": "\"Make mouse studies work.\"",
  "endpoint_class": "mixed",
  "endpoint_evidence": "\"All had been shown to ameliorate disease in an established animal model. All but one failed in the clinic...\" and \"The recommendations... include: rigorously assessing animals’ physical and biochemical traits in terms of human disease; characterizing when disease symptoms and death occur...\""
}
